Rajesh Sirigireddy, MSHI 
1 of 6
 
Public Comment On The Proposed Rule For Health Data Exchange And Drug 
Prior Authorization 
TO: 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) 
Department of Health and Human Services 
7500 Security Boulevard 
Baltimore, Maryland 21244 
 
FROM: 
Rajesh Sirigireddy 
Sacramento, California  
healthdataanalyst@gmail.com 
  
DATE: 
June 15, 2025 
 
SUBJECT: Public Comment on Proposed Rule for Health Data Exchange and Drug 
Prior Authorization 
To the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), 
I am submitting this public comment regarding the proposed rule on health data 
exchange and drug prior authorization. I want to express my strong support for the 
vision behind this initiative. The modernization of how healthcare data is shared and 
how insurance approvals are managed is not merely important; it is crucial and urgent. 
Effective and timely communication among payers, providers, and patients is essential 
for improving patient care and reducing unnecessary treatment delays. 
However, I believe that the success of this rule will largely depend on its 
implementation. After careful consideration, I would like to propose a recommendation 
that I feel could turn this initiative into a truly transformative effort rather than a mere 
incremental change. 
I urge that this rule proceed only if the following conditions are met: 
1. All prior regulatory implementations and existing deadlines must be successfully 
completed and stabilized before this new rule takes effect. 
2. All technology systems: across payers, providers, and government entities must be 
upgraded and validated to current standards before parallel implementation timelines 
begin. 
 
 
Rajesh Sirigireddy, MSHI 
2 of 6
 
3. Implementation must be carefully coordinated to avoid overlapping, conflicting 
efforts that waste resources and dilute focus. 
If these conditions are satisfied, this rule makes complete sense and creates genuine 
win-win outcomes for all state payers, providers, clinics, and patients. If implemented 
without these safeguards, parallel efforts will drain organizational energy, create 
inefficiencies, and fail to deliver the real-time, fruitful outcomes this rule promises. 
The goal is not incremental progress it is transformational, coordinated change that 
benefits everyone. That requires discipline, planning, and a commitment to getting the 
foundation right first. 
Below, I have provided a detailed analysis of the benefits and challenges across all 
stakeholder levels, along with specific recommendations for implementation success.  
 
Detailed Analysis: 
The proposed rule aims to modernize how healthcare data is shared and how 
insurance approvals (prior authorizations) for drugs are handled. While the goal is to 
make the system faster and more transparent, there are several "hidden" pain points 
and trade-offs for payers, clinics, and patients. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Rajesh Sirigireddy, MSHI 
3 of 6
 
Payer and Health Plan Level 
Pros: 
Fewer wasted requests: Real-time tools will tell providers immediately if an approval 
is even needed, which could stop plans from having to process thousands of 
unnecessary or duplicate requests. 
Better data quality: Receiving data in a standardized electronic format reduces the 
manual work needed to track down missing information. 
Hidden Pain Points (Cons): 
Overlapping build timelines: The proposed deadline of October 1, 2027, overlaps 
with existing technology requirements from previous rules. This means software 
developers may have to build two complex systems at the same time, which could 
double implementation costs in the short term. 
Government/State budget hurdles: For state Medicaid programs, meeting these 
deadlines depends on state legislatures approving money and the slow process of 
hiring outside contractors. 
Audit and penalty risks: A new "failure to report" rule would allow the government to 
fine companies if they don't provide documents quickly enough (within 30 days) during 
an audit. 
System maintenance: Beyond the initial multi-million dollar build, plans must pay for 
permanent technical support, estimated at 25% of the original build cost every year. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Rajesh Sirigireddy, MSHI 
4 of 6
 
Clinic and Provider Level 
Pros: 
Massive time savings: Electronic systems could cut the time spent on a single 
approval request from 24 minutes (manual) or 16 minutes (web portal) down to just 5 
or 6 minutes. 
No more guessing: Providers can see coverage rules directly inside their electronic 
health record (EHR) while they are still in the room with the patient. 
Clearer denials: Plans must give a specific reason for saying "no," which helps the 
clinic fix errors or pick a different medication without playing phone tag. 
Hidden Pain Points (Cons): 
Software upgrade costs: Most of these benefits only work if a clinic pays to upgrade 
to "certified" EHR technology, which can cost $10,000 or more just for the upgrade. 
Technical confusion: Clinics will have to navigate two different technical systems 
depending on how the drug is paid for: one system for drugs given in the office 
(medical benefit) and another for drugs picked up at a pharmacy (pharmacy benefit). 
Small practice gap: Smaller or rural clinics with older software may be left behind if 
their software vendors choose not to build these expensive new features. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Rajesh Sirigireddy, MSHI 
5 of 6
 
Patient Level 
Pros: 
Faster access to medicine: Standardized deadlines mean plans must respond to 
urgent drug requests within 24 hours and standard requests within 72 hours, reducing 
dangerous delays in starting treatment. 
Portable records: If a patient changes jobs or insurance plans, their data (including 
existing drug approvals) can follow them, so they don't have to start the approval 
process over from scratch. 
Better personal tools: Patients can use health apps of their choice to see exactly where 
their drug approval stands and what information might be missing. 
Hidden Pain Points (Cons): 
Cybersecurity risks: Sharing more data through more "digital doors" (APIs) 
increases the risk of hacking, ransomware, and identity theft. 
Privacy burden: Patients are responsible for vetting the apps they use. If they choose 
an app with poor privacy rules, their sensitive health data could be shared in ways they 
didn't intend. 
Broken connections: If a health plan’s technology is set up incorrectly, the patient 
might see "broken" data or lose access to their records until a software update is 
pushed. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Rajesh Sirigireddy, MSHI 
6 of 6
 
Overall Effect on Care 
The rule moves healthcare toward a "synchronous" model where doctors and 
insurance companies communicate instantly. The pro is a smoother experience where 
patients leave the doctor's office knowing their medicine is already approved. The con 
is a heavy reliance on a digital infrastructure that is expensive to build and remains a 
major target for cyberattacks that could disrupt care for entire hospital systems

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Rajesh Sirigireddy, MSHI
- **Stakeholder type:** Individual; Technology/health data professional
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** MSHI; health data analyst.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The commenter strongly supports CMS' vision for modernizing health data exchange and drug prior authorization but urges CMS to sequence implementation carefully. He recommends proceeding only after prior regulatory implementations are stabilized, technology systems across payers/providers/government are upgraded and validated, and overlapping timelines are coordinated to avoid wasted resources and implementation failure.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; API-USAGE-METRICS; OPEN-PAYMENTS-CMP; PRIVACY-SECURITY; GENERAL.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** Docket/proposed rule described generally; no CFR citations.
- **Standards referenced:** FHIR APIs, EHR technology, medical benefit vs pharmacy benefit PA systems, API-based patient data access.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Conditional support for modernization**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Support/Modify
- **Rationale:** The commenter says the initiative is crucial and urgent, but transformational success depends on stabilizing existing regulatory implementation and technology foundations first.
- **Specific request:** Proceed only after previous requirements/deadlines are completed, systems are upgraded and validated, and implementation is coordinated.

**Topic 2: Implementation timeline and overlapping builds**
- **Provision ID:** IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** The October 1, 2027 deadline overlaps with existing technology requirements, potentially doubling short-term costs and stretching state budgets, contractor procurement, and software development.
- **Specific request:** Avoid parallel implementation timelines that conflict with existing rules and drain implementation capacity.

**Topic 3: Provider/clinic impact**
- **Provision ID:** PROVIDER-BURDEN; MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT; PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Support/Concerned
- **Rationale:** Electronic systems can reduce PA time and provide coverage rules inside EHRs, but clinics may need expensive software upgrades and must navigate separate medical-benefit and pharmacy-benefit systems.
- **Specific request:** Ensure providers, including small and rural clinics, are not left behind by EHR upgrade costs or technical confusion.

**Topic 4: Patient benefits and privacy/cyber risks**
- **Provision ID:** PATIENT-ACCESS; PRIVACY-SECURITY
- **Position:** Support/Concerned
- **Rationale:** Faster PA decisions, portable records, and patient apps can improve access, but increased API data sharing raises cybersecurity and privacy risks and can create broken connections.
- **Specific request:** Strengthen implementation safeguards for cybersecurity, privacy, and reliable patient-facing data connections.

**Topic 5: Audit and penalty exposure**
- **Provision ID:** OPEN-PAYMENTS-CMP
- **Position:** Concerned
- **Rationale:** The commenter notes that failure-to-report rules may create audit and penalty risks if documents are not produced quickly enough.
- **Specific request:** Ensure audit expectations are realistic and do not add destabilizing penalty risk during implementation.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S12/S15:** The commenter notes technical confusion from two systems depending on whether drugs are paid under medical or pharmacy benefit.
- **S18/S21/S37:** The commenter raises implementation burden and timeline concerns for payers, clinics, state programs, and software developers.
- **S20/S43:** The comment references 24-hour urgent and 72-hour standard deadlines as patient access benefits.
- **S23/S30:** The commenter highlights cybersecurity, ransomware, identity theft, and patient privacy risks associated with expanded APIs.
- **S48/S49:** The comment discusses costs, especially payer build costs, ongoing maintenance, clinic software upgrades, and small/rural clinic gaps.
- **S57-S59:** The comment touches on audit/penalty risk under a failure-to-report concept.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Stabilize all prior regulatory implementations before this new rule takes effect.
2. Upgrade and validate payer, provider, and government technology systems to current standards before parallel implementation.
3. Coordinate implementation timelines to avoid overlapping and conflicting work.
4. Account for state budget and contractor procurement hurdles.
5. Support clinics facing EHR upgrade costs and prevent small/rural practices from being left behind.
6. Address cybersecurity, privacy, and app-vetting risks created by expanded APIs.
7. Ensure audit and penalty structures are workable.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Overlapping deadlines, doubled implementation costs, state budget/procurement constraints, ongoing maintenance expenses, clinic software upgrade costs, cybersecurity, privacy, broken data connections.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Inefficiency, resource dilution, small/rural clinic gaps, patient privacy exposure, cyberattack disruptions, failure to achieve real-time outcomes.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Concurrent software builds, state legislative funding, contractor hiring, certified EHR upgrades, dual benefit-specific systems.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** PA request time could drop from 24 minutes manual or 16 minutes web portal to 5-6 minutes electronically; EHR upgrades may cost $10,000 or more; ongoing support may be 25% of original build cost annually.
- **Studies or research referenced:** Not cited.
- **Examples provided:** Separate technical systems for drugs given in office versus drugs picked up at pharmacy; patient apps and API digital doors increasing privacy/cyber risk.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Payers, state Medicaid programs, software developers, clinics, providers, small/rural practices, patients.
- **Economic implications:** Multi-million-dollar initial builds, ongoing support costs, EHR upgrade costs, budget/contractor constraints.
- **Technical feasibility:** Feasible only with sequenced, validated, coordinated implementation and upgraded systems.
- **Patient care impact:** Potential for faster medicine access and portable records, but risks from failed implementation, broken connections, and cybersecurity disruptions.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive but conditional/concerned.
- **Tone:** Practical, implementation-focused, cautionary.
- **Priority level:** Medium-High.

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "I want to express my strong support for the vision behind this initiative." - Context: Opening support for modernization.
2. "The success of this rule will largely depend on its implementation." - Context: Central thesis of the comment.
3. "All prior regulatory implementations and existing deadlines must be successfully completed and stabilized before this new rule takes effect." - Context: Primary sequencing recommendation.
4. "The goal is not incremental progress it is transformational, coordinated change that benefits everyone." - Context: Rationale for coordinated implementation.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - The comment centers on avoiding overlapping and conflicting implementation timelines.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - Discusses build costs, maintenance, EHR upgrades, and state budget hurdles.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Emphasizes system validation and readiness before parallel implementation.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Notes provider time savings but also clinic software costs and workflow complexity.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Highlights faster access, portable records, and patient app visibility.
- [x] **PRIVACY-SECURITY** - Discusses cybersecurity, ransomware, identity theft, and patient app privacy.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - Identifies confusion from separate technical systems.
- [x] **SMALL-PAYER-IMPACT** - Discusses small/rural clinics; small payer impact is less direct but resource-limited entities are a core concern.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Focuses on practical rollout across current payer/provider systems.
- [ ] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - Not directly addressed.
- [ ] **REGULATORY-AUTHORITY** - Not addressed.
- [ ] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Implicit and important, but not deeply developed beyond coordination.
- [ ] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - Not directly addressed.
- [ ] **TRANSPARENCY** - Mentioned through clearer denials and apps, not central.
- [ ] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - Software developers mentioned but not the main frame.
